Title: The Extra Change
Dilemma: You buy a snack at the store. The cashier is in a hurry and gives you a ten-dollar bill back instead of a one-dollar bill. Nobody noticed, and you could really use the money.
Question: Is it okay to keep the extra money, since it was the cashier's mistake and not yours?
Right Choice: Return the money
Wrong Choice: Keep the money
Catholic Answer: No. Keeping money you know is not yours is a form of taking what belongs to someone else, even if you did nothing to cause the mistake. The Catechism lists knowingly keeping what is not ours, such as lost objects or money given in error, as a sin against the Seventh Commandment. The cashier may even have to pay back the missing money out of their own pocket. The right thing to do is to point out the mistake and give back the extra money right away. Honesty in small things builds the habit of honesty in big things (Luke 16:10).
Key Principle: Justice: give each person what is rightfully theirs; we may not keep what we know belongs to another.
Sources: CCC 2409 (Holy See): https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P8B.HTM

Title: The Lost Wallet
Dilemma: Walking home from school, you find a wallet on the sidewalk with forty dollars and a driver's license inside. Your friend says, "Finders keepers! Nobody will ever know."
Question: Do you have to try to return it, or can you keep what you found?
Right Choice: Return the wallet to its owner
Wrong Choice: Keep the wallet and the cash
Catholic Answer: You must make an honest effort to return it. A lost item still belongs to its owner, and deliberately keeping it is a sin against the Seventh Commandment. Here the owner is easy to find because the license has a name and address, so you could return it yourself with a parent, or take it to the police or a teacher. Traditional Catholic teaching says that the more valuable the item, the harder we must try to find the owner, and only after sincere efforts fail may we keep it. Returning it is also a great act of love for your neighbor, who is probably worried.
Key Principle: Lost property still belongs to its owner; justice requires a real effort to return it.
Sources: The Wanderer, "Accounting to St. Peter": https://thewandererpress.com/catholic/news/frontpage/accounting-to-st-peter/ ; Opus Dei, Topic 36: Seventh Commandment: https://opusdei.org/en/article/topic-36-seventh-commandment/

Title: Can I Copy Your Homework?
Dilemma: Your best friend forgot to do the math homework and begs to copy yours before class. If you say no, your friend will be upset and might get a bad grade.
Question: Is letting a friend copy your work a kind thing to do, or is it wrong?
Right Choice: Say no, and offer to help your friend learn it
Wrong Choice: Let your friend copy your homework
Catholic Answer: Letting a friend copy is not truly kind, because it helps them deceive the teacher and pass off your work as their own. Cheating is a form of dishonesty and unfairness to the teacher and to the other students who did the work. When we help someone else do something wrong, we share in their wrongdoing. Real friendship wants what is truly good for the other person, so you could offer to help your friend understand the problems at lunch, or encourage them to be honest with the teacher. Saying no kindly is an act of love.
Key Principle: Truthfulness and justice; we may not help others sin, and real charity wills the true good of another.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Ugly Sweater
Dilemma: Your grandmother knitted you a sweater for your birthday. You think it is ugly and scratchy. She smiles and asks, "Do you love it?"
Question: Should you tell a "white lie" and say you love it, to spare her feelings?
Right Choice: Thank her truthfully for her love and hard work
Wrong Choice: Tell her you love the sweater
Catholic Answer: The Church teaches that lying, which is speaking a falsehood in order to deceive, is wrong by its very nature, though small lies are usually venial sins and not mortal ones. But honesty does not require being rude. You can say true and loving things: you love that she made it for you, you can see how much work went into it, and you are grateful she thought of you. Charity and respect for the truth should guide every answer we give. With a little thought, we can almost always find something both true and kind to say.
Key Principle: Never lie, but speak the truth with charity and tact.
Sources: OSV, "Are little white lies okay to tell?": https://www.oursundayvisitor.com/are-little-white-lies-okay-to-tell/ ; Catholic Encyclopedia, "Lying": https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/lying

Title: The Surprise Party
Dilemma: Your family is planning a surprise party for your mom. She notices you whispering and asks, "What are you all up to?"
Question: How do you keep the surprise without telling a lie?
Right Choice: Say it's a secret, or change the subject
Wrong Choice: Make up a false story to cover it
Catholic Answer: Keeping a good secret is not the same as lying. The Catechism teaches that we are not always required to reveal everything we know, and that we may keep silent or use discreet language when there is a good reason. You might say, "It's a secret, you'll find out soon!" or simply change the subject with a smile. What you should avoid is making up a false story, like saying you were talking about homework. A happy surprise is a good reason to keep quiet, and it can be done without deceiving anyone.
Key Principle: We may keep silent or be discreet for a good reason, but we may not deceive by lying.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Is Lying a Sin if Done to Protect Someone from Death?" (discussion of CCC 2488-2489): https://www.catholic.com/qa/is-lying-a-sin-if-done-to-protect-someone-from-death

Title: The Sunday Tournament
Dilemma: Your soccer team made it to the championship tournament. The final game is Sunday morning, at the same time as Mass, and the coach says everyone must be there.
Question: Is a big game a good enough reason to miss Sunday Mass?
Right Choice: Go to a Mass that fits, even if it means missing the game
Wrong Choice: Skip Mass to play the game
Catholic Answer: Sunday Mass is a serious obligation, and missing it on purpose without a serious reason is a grave sin. Serious reasons are things like illness or caring for a small baby, not sports or fun activities. But there are usually good options: go to the Saturday evening vigil Mass, which fulfills the Sunday obligation, or find a Mass near the tournament at a different time. If there is truly no way to get to Mass, the family should put God first, even if that means missing a game. Making the effort is a strong witness of faith to teammates.
Key Principle: Keep holy the Lord's Day; Sunday Mass comes before games and entertainment.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Missing Mass on a Sunday or Other Holy Day of Obligation": https://www.catholic.com/qa/missing-mass-on-a-holy-day-of-obligation ; The Catholic Spirit, "When sports clash with Sunday Mass": https://thecatholicspirit.com/special-sections/back-to-school/sports-clash-sunday-mass-whats-parent/

Title: The Bystander
Dilemma: At recess, some kids are making fun of a classmate and knocking his books down. You are not joining in, but you are afraid that if you step in, they will pick on you next.
Question: If you are not the one doing the bullying, have you done anything wrong by just watching?
Right Choice: Speak up safely, tell an adult, and befriend him
Wrong Choice: Stay quiet and just watch
Catholic Answer: Staying silent can make us share in someone else's wrongdoing. The Catechism says we can cooperate in the sins of others by approving of them or by not stopping them when we have a duty to do so. You do not have to put yourself in danger, but you should do something safe and loving: refuse to laugh along, tell a teacher or another trusted adult, and be a friend to the classmate afterward by sitting with him or helping pick up his books. Comforting those who suffer is one of the works of mercy.
Key Principle: Love of neighbor; we must not cooperate in the sins of others, even by silent approval.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: Is it Gossip if it is True?
Dilemma: You find out that a classmate got caught shoplifting last summer. Some friends ask if you know anything juicy about her. You say, "Well, it's true, so it's not really gossip."
Question: If something bad about a person is true, is it okay to tell others?
Right Choice: Keep her past to yourself
Wrong Choice: Tell your friends what she did
Catholic Answer: No. Telling others about someone's real faults or sins without a good and serious reason is a sin called detraction. Even when it is true, it hurts the person's good name, which is very hard to repair. If the story is false, it is even worse, a sin called calumny. A good reason to share might be keeping someone safe, such as telling a parent or teacher about danger, but not entertaining friends. We should speak about others the way we would want them to speak about us.
Key Principle: Respect for every person's reputation; we may not reveal another's faults without a valid reason.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Dangerous Secret
Dilemma: Your close friend tells you she has been hurting herself, and makes you promise not to tell anyone, especially not an adult.
Question: Should you keep the promise, or break it to get her help?
Right Choice: Tell a trusted adult so she gets help
Wrong Choice: Keep the promise and tell no one
Catholic Answer: Normally we should keep secrets that others trust us with. But the Catechism teaches that a secret does not have to be kept when keeping it would cause very grave harm to the person who shared it or to someone else. Your friend's safety and life matter more than the promise. The loving thing is to tell a trusted adult, such as a parent, school counselor, or priest, as soon as possible, even if your friend is upset at first. Keep being her friend, pray for her, and let her know you told because you care about her.
Key Principle: Secrets must be kept, except when keeping them would cause very grave harm.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Heinz Dilemma
Dilemma: A man's wife is dying, and only one expensive drug can save her. The druggist who invented it charges ten times what it costs to make. The man begs for a lower price or a payment plan, but is refused. In desperation, he breaks in and steals the drug.
Question: Was he wrong to steal the drug to save his wife's life?
Right Choice: Seek help from everyone, and take the drug only as a last resort to save her life
Wrong Choice: Let her die, because the druggist's profit comes first
Catholic Answer: Stealing is wrong, but the Church recognizes that taking another's goods is not theft when someone is in obvious and urgent need and the only way to meet an essential need is to use what belongs to another. The goods of the earth are meant by God for everyone, and owners are stewards who must share them with those in need. So the man's action has serious mitigating circumstances and may even be justified. Still, he should first try every other way: asking the community, the parish, and charities for help. The druggist also has a serious duty to make his life-saving drug available.
Key Principle: The universal destination of goods; extreme necessity changes what counts as theft.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "A Moral Assessment of 'The Heinz Dilemma'": https://www.catholic.com/qa/a-moral-assessment-of-the-heinz-dilemma

Title: The Intruder
Dilemma: In the middle of the night, an armed intruder breaks into your home and threatens your family. The only way to stop him may be to seriously injure or even kill him.
Question: Is it a sin to use deadly force to defend yourself and your family?
Right Choice: Defend your family, using only the force needed to stop him
Wrong Choice: Do whatever you want to him; he deserves it
Catholic Answer: No, the Church teaches that legitimate defense is allowed, and that for those responsible for others, like a parent, it can be a serious duty. Following St. Thomas Aquinas, the act has two effects: protecting life and harming the attacker. The goal must be to stop the attack, not to kill for its own sake. A person must use only as much force as is needed, so if the intruder can be stopped by lesser means, those should be used. If the attacker dies as a result of necessary defense, the defender is not guilty of murder.
Key Principle: Legitimate defense; love for oneself and duty to protect others, using only necessary force.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Confession of a Crime
Dilemma: A man confesses to a priest that he committed a terrible crime. Another person has been arrested and blamed for it. The priest is the only one who knows the truth.
Question: Should the priest go to the police to free the innocent person?
Right Choice: Keep the seal, and urge the man to turn himself in
Wrong Choice: Tell the police what the man confessed
Catholic Answer: No. The seal of confession is absolute: a priest may never reveal anything he learns in confession, for any reason, under penalty of excommunication. This protects every person's freedom to confess sins to God without fear. The priest can urge the penitent to turn himself in, make things right, and free the innocent person, and he may offer to go with him. According to Catholic Answers, the priest may not refuse absolution to force the person to go to the police, though he may withhold it if the penitent is not truly sorry. Several priests in history died rather than break the seal.
Key Principle: The sacramental seal of confession is inviolable.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Can Absolution Be Withheld from a Murderer Until He Agrees to Give Himself Up?": https://www.catholic.com/qa/can-absolution-be-withheld-from-a-murderer-until-he-agrees-to-give-himself-up-to-authorities ; Catholic Answers, "Priestly Responsibility Regarding Crimes Confessed": https://www.catholic.com/qa/priestly-responsibility-regarding-crimes-confessed

Title: The Boss's Request
Dilemma: You have a part-time job. Your manager asks you to change the dates on expired food labels so the store does not lose money. He says it is "company policy" and you could lose your job if you refuse.
Question: If your boss orders it, are you still responsible?
Right Choice: Refuse, even if it costs you the job
Wrong Choice: Change the labels as ordered
Catholic Answer: Yes. Following orders does not excuse us from doing something wrong. Falsifying labels is fraud and could make customers sick, which is a serious injustice. Directly carrying out a wrong act yourself, or sharing in the wrongdoer's intention, is never allowed. The Catechism teaches that we must always obey the certain judgment of a well-formed conscience. You should respectfully refuse, explain why, and, if needed, report the problem to someone higher up, even if it costs you the job. God sees and rewards those who choose integrity.
Key Principle: Never formally cooperate in evil; obey a well-formed conscience over unjust orders.
Sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, "Accomplice" (formal and material cooperation): https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/accomplice ; National Catholic Bioethics Center, "The Courage to Refuse to Cooperate in Evil": https://www.ncbcenter.org/making-sense-of-bioethics-cms/column-070-the-courage-to-refuse-to-cooperate-in-evil

Title: The Kidney for a Brother
Dilemma: Your older brother's kidneys are failing. Tests show that you are a perfect match. Doctors say you can live a healthy life with one kidney, but surgery always has some risk.
Question: Is it right to give away part of your own body, and are you required to?
Right Choice: Donate freely as a gift of love, if you prayerfully choose to
Wrong Choice: Refuse, because giving away part of your body is a sin
Catholic Answer: Donating an organ while alive can be a beautiful act of generous love, and the Church allows it when the risks to the donor are proportionate to the good done for the person who receives it. The donor must give free and informed consent; no one may be forced or pressured. It is an act of charity, not a strict obligation, so a person may prayerfully decide either way. What is never allowed is a donation that would directly cause the donor's death or disabling mutilation, or selling organs for money.
Key Principle: Organ donation is a noble gift when the risk is proportionate and consent is free.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Ticking Bomb
Dilemma: Police have captured a terrorist who planted a bomb somewhere in a city. It will explode in a few hours and kill thousands. He refuses to say where it is. An officer suggests torturing him to get the information.
Question: Can torture be justified if it might save thousands of lives?
Right Choice: Refuse to torture him; use only lawful means
Wrong Choice: Torture him to find the bomb
Catholic Answer: No. The Catechism teaches that torture, which uses physical or moral violence to extract confessions, punish, frighten, or satisfy hatred, is contrary to respect for human dignity. St. John Paul II listed torture among acts that are intrinsically evil, which means they can never be justified by good intentions or good results. The U.S. bishops have taught the same, calling torture intrinsically evil. Even a guilty person keeps the dignity of a child of God. Society must use every legitimate means, but never evil means, to protect innocent life.
Key Principle: Some acts are intrinsically evil and can never be done, whatever the consequences.
Sources: USCCB, "Torture is an Intrinsic Evil": https://www.usccb.org/resources/torture-intrinsic-evil-catholic-study-guide-one-session-workshop ; USCCB, "Background on Torture": https://www.usccb.org/resources/background-torture-february-2013

Title: The Ventilator
Dilemma: Your grandfather has terminal cancer and is now on a ventilator. Doctors say the machine will not cure him and only prolongs his dying, which is causing him great burden. Your family must decide whether to remove it.
Question: Would removing the ventilator be the same as euthanasia?
Right Choice: Remove the ventilator, but keep caring for him
Wrong Choice: Give him a lethal dose to end it faster
Catholic Answer: No. The Church teaches that we must always provide ordinary care, but we are not required to use medical procedures that are burdensome, extraordinary, or disproportionate to the expected result. Stopping such treatment is not choosing to kill; it is accepting that death can no longer be prevented. The decision belongs to the patient if he is able to decide, or to those legally entitled to act for him. Normal care, comfort, pain relief, and, in principle, food and water must continue. The family should also call a priest for the sacraments.
Key Principle: Ordinary means must be used; extraordinary or disproportionate means may be refused.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Church Teaching on End-of-Life Care": https://www.catholic.com/qa/church-teaching-on-end-of-life-care ; National Catholic Bioethics Center, "Turning Off a Ventilator versus Withdrawing Assisted Nutrition and Hydration": https://www.ncbcenter.org/messages-from-presidents/turningoffaventilator

Title: "Please Help Me Die"
Dilemma: An elderly woman with a painful illness lives in a place where assisted suicide is legal. She tells her family she does not want to be a burden and asks them to support her request for a lethal prescription.
Question: Is it merciful to help someone end their life to stop their suffering?
Right Choice: Stay with her and get her good pain care
Wrong Choice: Help her get the lethal prescription
Catholic Answer: No. The Church teaches that any act or omission that by itself or by intention causes death in order to end suffering is a grave offense against the dignity of the person and against God. True mercy means staying with the suffering person, not eliminating them. Palliative care is encouraged: doctors may give strong painkillers to relieve pain, even if they might shorten life, as long as death is not intended. The family can reassure her that she is loved and never a burden, and help her receive the sacraments.
Key Principle: Life is a gift from God; euthanasia and assisted suicide are never permitted, but pain relief is.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Church Teaching on End-of-Life Care": https://www.catholic.com/qa/church-teaching-on-end-of-life-care

Title: The Unjust Order
Dilemma: A soldier at war is ordered by his commander to open fire on a village full of unarmed civilians as punishment for an enemy attack. Refusing could mean being arrested or worse.
Question: Is a soldier guilty if he is only following orders?
Right Choice: Refuse to fire on the civilians
Wrong Choice: Obey the order and fire
Catholic Answer: Yes. The Catechism teaches that actions deliberately contrary to the law of nations, and the orders that command them, are crimes, and that blind obedience does not excuse those who carry them out. Deliberately killing non-combatants is always gravely wrong. The soldier has a duty to refuse, even at great personal cost. Citizens and soldiers are obliged in conscience not to follow commands that are contrary to the moral order.
Key Principle: Moral law binds even in war; unjust orders must be refused.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Lifeboat
Dilemma: After a shipwreck, a lifeboat built for ten people holds twelve, and it is starting to sink. Someone suggests throwing two of the weakest passengers overboard so the rest can survive.
Question: May the group sacrifice two people to save ten?
Right Choice: Refuse to throw anyone overboard
Wrong Choice: Throw the two weakest overboard
Catholic Answer: No. Throwing innocent people overboard would be directly killing them, which is always gravely wrong no matter how many lives might be saved. We may never do evil so that good may come of it. However, a person may freely choose to give up his own place out of love, which is very different from killing. Jesus said that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. St. Maximilian Kolbe did this at Auschwitz when he offered his life in place of another prisoner.
Key Principle: Direct killing of the innocent is never allowed, but freely laying down one's own life out of love is heroic.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Jury Room
Dilemma: You serve on a jury in a murder trial and the defendant is clearly guilty of a terrible crime. Now the jury must choose between life in prison and the death penalty.
Question: What does the Church teach about the death penalty today?
Right Choice: Vote for life in prison
Wrong Choice: Vote for the death penalty
Catholic Answer: In 2018, Pope Francis revised the Catechism to teach that, in light of the Gospel, the death penalty is inadmissible because it attacks the dignity of the person, and the Church works for its abolition worldwide. The Catechism explains that modern prisons can protect society while still giving the guilty a chance to repent. This does not mean the crime is unimportant: justice and punishment are real duties of the state, and victims deserve care. A Catholic juror can support a just punishment that protects the public, such as life in prison, while respecting human dignity.
Key Principle: Every human life, even the guilty, has dignity; punishment must protect society without taking life.
Sources: CCC 2267 as revised in 2018 (Holy See); USCCB statements on the death penalty

Title: The Ectopic Pregnancy
Dilemma: A young mother learns that her pregnancy is ectopic: her baby has implanted in her fallopian tube instead of her uterus. The baby cannot survive there, and the tube may burst and cause life-threatening bleeding. Doctors recommend surgery to remove the damaged part of the tube, and the baby will not survive.
Question: Is removing the damaged tube the same as an abortion?
Right Choice: Remove the damaged tube to save the mother's life
Wrong Choice: Refuse the surgery, since it is the same as an abortion
Catholic Answer: No. Direct abortion, willed as an end or a means, is always gravely wrong, and the U.S. bishops' Ethical and Religious Directives (Directive 48) say that in an ectopic pregnancy no treatment that is a direct abortion is allowed. But Catholic ethicists agree that removing the damaged section of the tube (a salpingectomy) is permitted under the principle of double effect. The surgery treats the mother's life-threatening condition, and the baby's death is foreseen but not intended, and it is not the means by which the mother is saved. Other treatments, such as the drug methotrexate or removing only the embryo while leaving the tube in place, are still debated among faithful Catholic ethicists. In every case the baby is a real person to be loved, mourned, and prayed for.
Key Principle: Double effect distinguishes treating a deadly condition, with a tragic side effect, from directly taking an innocent life.
Sources: USCCB, Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services, Directive 48; Catholic Voice (Archdiocese of Omaha), "Dispelling fears about pregnancy complications and abortion restrictions": https://catholicvoiceomaha.com/dispelling-fears-about-pregnancy-complications-and-abortion-restrictions/ ; Catholic Health Association, "Catholic Hospitals and Ectopic Pregnancies": https://chausa.org/publications/health-care-ethics-usa/article/winter-2011/catholic-hospitals-and-ectopic-pregnancies

Title: The Atomic Bomb
Dilemma: In August 1945, near the end of World War II, U.S. leaders decided to drop atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing well over 200,000 people, most of them civilians. Defenders argued it would force a quick surrender and avoid an invasion that might have cost far more lives on both sides.
Question: Can destroying whole cities full of civilians be justified if it ends a war sooner and saves more lives overall?
Right Choice: Never target cities full of civilians
Wrong Choice: Drop the bombs to end the war faster
Catholic Answer: No. The Second Vatican Council taught, and the Catechism repeats, that any act of war aimed at the indiscriminate destruction of whole cities and their people is a grave sin against God and man that deserves firm and unhesitating condemnation. The deliberate killing of non-combatants is always gravely wrong, even in a just war. Here the deaths of innocent men, women, and children were not a side effect but the very means used to pressure Japan to surrender, so the principle of double effect cannot apply; it is the same error as pushing the man off the bridge. We may never do evil so that good may come of it. Nagasaki was the historic heart of Catholic Japan, and the bomb destroyed its cathedral and killed thousands of Catholics. Visiting Hiroshima in 2019, Pope Francis declared that using atomic energy for war is immoral, and so is possessing nuclear weapons.
Key Principle: Deliberately targeting civilians is always a grave sin; a good end can never justify an evil means.
Sources: Pope Francis, Meeting for Peace, Hiroshima (24 November 2019): https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2019/november/documents/papa-francesco_20191124_messaggio-incontropace-hiroshima.html ; Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 80: http://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vatii_cons_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html
